# Draft:Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre

Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre
The [https://canadianindustrialheritage.com/ Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre] (CIHC) is a cultural and heritage organization in Canada dedicated to the preservation, interpretation, and public presentation of the country’s industrial heritage. The organization focuses on exploring how industrial development has influenced Canadian society, including its effects on communities, labour practices, technology, and the built environment
The centre works to collect, preserve, and interpret historical materials related to Canada’s industrial past. These may include archival records, photographs, correspondence, and other documentary sources that provide insight into the development of manufacturing, trade, and industry. Through research initiatives public-facing projects, CIHC seeks to make these materials more accessible to researchers, students, and the general public.
Although the organization does not maintain a permanent public facility, its operations are based in Brantford, Ontario, a city historically associated with manufacturing and industrial innovation. From this base, the centre collaborates with community partners heritage organizations, and private collections to support the preservation and study of industrial history.
CIHC also participates in digital heritage initiatives, including the transcription and interpretation of historical documents and the development of online resources that highlight Canada’s industrial and commercial history. These efforts aim to increase public awareness of the role industry has played in shaping regional economies, urban development, and everyday life.
The organization’s work contributes to broader discussions about heritage preservation, historical research, and the cultural legacy of industrialization in Canada.
History
The [https://canadianindustrialheritage.com/ Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre] (CIHC) was established to address the growing need to preserve industrial sites, practices, and narratives that have played a significant role in Canadian history. Its formation reflects broader heritage conservation efforts that recognize industrial landscapes, infrastructure, and manufacturing traditions as important cultural resources, particularly as many former industrial sites face redevelopment or demolition.
The organization traces its origins to the Cockshutt Homecoming Festival, held in June 2000 at Cockshutt Park in Brantford, Ontario. The event brought together approximately 6,500 attendees from across Canada, the United States, and other countries to celebrate the history of the Cockshutt Plow Company, a major manufacturer historically based in Brantford. During the festival, organizers and community members established the Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre with the aim of preserving and interpreting the city’s industrial heritage.
One of the organization’s early objectives was the restoration of the former Cockshutt Plow Company Main Office, an important site connected to the company’s operations. Plans to restore the building were halted when the structure was later destroyed by fire. Following the loss of the Main Office, the organization shifted its focus toward preserving other remaining industrial structures associated with the Cockshutt complex.
In subsequent years, CIHC worked with the City of Brantford to support the preservation and interpretation of remaining heritage structures, including the Time Keeper’s Office located at 66 Mohawk Street. Structural assessments of the building were commissioned as part of efforts to evaluate its condition and explore possibilities for conservation. The organization also collaborated with the architecture firm MMMC in developing plans for a future heritage and cultural space associated with the site. The area later came under review by the Survivors Secretariat due to its historical connection to land that had previously been used as a farm area for the former Mohawk Residential School.
Since its founding, the centre has supported research, documentation, and public awareness initiatives related to industrial heritage. These activities have included collaborations with historians, community groups, and heritage professionals to record and interpret industrial histories that may otherwise receive limited attention within traditional heritage frameworks.
CIHC has also undertaken publishing and documentation initiatives related to local and industrial history. In 2005 the organization published Cockshutt Plant News, a compilation of employee newsletters originally produced by the Cockshutt Plow Company during the Second World War. The centre has also produced its own newsletter since 2000, sharing research and updates related to industrial heritage.
Since 2019, the organization has collaborated with Brant Theatre Workshops, Wilfrid Laurier University’s Brantford campus, and the Brant Historical Society on the Memories of Brantford Immigrant Communities project. The initiative documents the experiences of immigrant communities in the city through public events and a digital archive known as the Memories website. Programs have highlighted the histories of Italian, Jewish, Chinese, and Ukrainian communities in Brantford.
Although the organization does not maintain a permanent public facility, its activities are coordinated from Brantford, Ontario.
Projects and Initiatives
The [https://canadianindustrialheritage.com/ Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre] (CIHC) has undertaken a number of research and community history initiatives that focus on documenting the industrial and social history of Brantford and the surrounding region. These projects typically combine archival research, oral history, and collaboration with local organizations to explore how industry, labour, and community development have shaped the region over time.
Roots of Eagle Place
Roots of Eagle Place is a community history project that examines the development of the Eagle Place neighbourhood in Brantford, Ontario. Historically a working-class district located near several manufacturing and industrial sites, Eagle Place developed alongside the growth of factories and transportation infrastructure in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The project documents the social and industrial history of the area, including the experiences of families who lived and worked in the neighbourhood and the role of nearby factories in shaping everyday life. Research associated with the initiative draws on archival records, photographs, and community recollections to explore the connections between industrial employment, neighbourhood identity, and urban development.
Women at Cockshutt Aircraft Division
The Women at Cockshutt Aircraft Division project focuses on the contributions of women who worked at the Cockshutt factory during the Second World War. During the war, sections of the Cockshutt manufacturing facilities in Brantford were adapted for aircraft-related production, including the manufacture of components for military aircraft. As many men were serving in the armed forces, women were recruited to work in industrial roles that had previously been dominated by male workers. The project examines the experiences of these women, documenting their work in wartime manufacturing and the broader social changes associated with women’s participation in industrial labour during the 1940s. Research for the project includes archival materials, photographs, and historical accounts related to wartime production in Brantford.
Waterous Engine Works
The Waterous Engine Works project documents the history of a manufacturing company associated with the production of firefighting equipment and industrial machinery. Waterous Engine Works was historically linked to the development of fire pumps and firefighting technologies that were used by fire departments across North America and internationally. CIHC’s research initiative examines the company’s operations, technological developments, and role within the broader industrial landscape of Brantford. The project also explores the relationship between industrial manufacturing and the development of municipal services such as firefighting and public safety.
Cockshutt Letter Book Project
The Cockshutt Letter Book Project is an archival initiative dedicated to the preservation and transcription of a nineteenth-century business letterbook associated with the Cockshutt firm. The letterbook, dating primarily from 1854, contains handwritten copies of outgoing correspondence related to commercial transactions, shipments of goods, financial arrangements, and business relationships with merchants and agents in other cities. These documents provide insight into the daily operations of a mid-nineteenth-century merchant enterprise and the trade networks that connected communities across Canada and beyond. The project involves the digitization and transcription of the handwritten records in order to make them accessible to researchers and the public, while also contributing to the documentation of early commercial history in Brantford.
Through these initiatives, the [https://canadianindustrialheritage.com/ Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre] contributes to the preservation and interpretation of industrial and community history, highlighting the ways in which manufacturing, labour, and commerce have shaped the development of the region.
Events and Exhibits
The [https://canadianindustrialheritage.com/ Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre] (CIHC) has organized and participated in a variety of public programs, including exhibitions, lectures, and symposiums focused on industrial and community history. These initiatives aim to present historical research to a broader audience and to encourage discussion about the social, economic, and cultural impacts of industry in the Brantford region.
Among the centre’s exhibitions is Inventors, Industries, and Marketing, which was developed as CIHC’s first pop-up exhibit. The exhibit explores the relationship between technological innovation, manufacturing, and marketing practices in Brantford’s industrial history, highlighting the ways local industries promoted their products and developed national and international markets.
Another exhibit, Fibres and Fabrics: Weaving Brantford’s Textile History, examines the development of textile production and related industries in the region. The exhibit presents historical materials and interpretive content related to the growth of textile manufacturing and its role in shaping employment and economic development in the city.
CIHC has also presented exhibitions focused on the city’s industrial contributions during the Second World War. Cockshutt Moulded Aircraft Factory examines wartime production associated with the Cockshutt manufacturing facilities in Brantford, including the production of components related to aircraft manufacturing. The exhibit explores the adaptation of existing industrial infrastructure for wartime needs and the role of local workers in supporting the war effort.
Another historically focused exhibit, Swords and Plowshares Revisited, examines the transition of industrial production from military to civilian uses. The exhibit highlights the ways manufacturers adapted wartime production technologies and facilities to peacetime manufacturing following the end of the Second World War.
In addition to exhibitions focused on industrial history, CIHC has participated in community-based heritage initiatives. Roots & Routes: Black Brantford — Freedom Seekers, Community Builders explores the history of Black communities in Brantford, including the experiences of freedom seekers who arrived in the region through networks connected to the Underground Railroad and the development of Black community institutions in the city.
CIHC has also supported public events and symposium-style gatherings that bring together historians, researchers, and community members to discuss topics related to industrial heritage and regional history. These events provide opportunities for presentations, discussions, and the sharing of research related to manufacturing history, labour, and community development in Brantford and surrounding areas.
Through these exhibitions and events, the centre has contributed to public engagement with local history and the interpretation of industrial heritage in the region.
Publications and Newsletters
The [https://canadianindustrialheritage.com/ Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre] (CIHC) has produced a number of publications and newsletters related to the documentation and interpretation of industrial and local history. These publications are intended to share research findings, historical materials, and updates on heritage initiatives with members of the public, researchers, and community partners.
In 2005 the organization published Cockshutt Plant News, a compilation of employee newsletters originally produced by the Cockshutt Plow Company during the Second World War. The newsletters were distributed to employees of the company and documented wartime production activities, workplace events, and community initiatives associated with the factory during the 1940s. The CIHC publication brought together these historical newsletters into a collected volume, providing researchers and readers with access to a primary source documenting industrial life in Brantford during the war years.
In addition to this publication, CIHC has produced its own newsletter since 2000. The newsletter has served as a means of sharing information about the organization’s activities, research projects, and collaborations with community partners. Issues have included articles on local industrial history, updates on heritage preservation efforts, and information about public events and educational initiatives organized by the centre.
Through these publications, the organization contributes to the documentation and dissemination of research related to industrial heritage in the Brantford region and Canada more broadly.
Partnerships and Collaborations
The [https://canadianindustrialheritage.com/ Canadian Industrial Heritage Centre] (CIHC) collaborates with a range of community organizations, cultural institutions, and academic partners in support of research, heritage preservation, and public programming related to industrial and community history. These partnerships contribute to the centre’s efforts to document historical materials, develop educational initiatives, and promote awareness of industrial heritage in Canada.
Community and institutional partners have included Brant Theatre Workshops, the Brant Historical Society, and Wilfrid Laurier University, as well as local heritage and cultural organizations such as the Eagle Place Neighbourhood Association, the Paris Museum and Historical Society, and the Waterford Heritage and AgriCanadianMuseum. The centre has also collaborated with research and archival organizations including the Ontario Genealogical Society and the Brantford Public Library.
CIHC has engaged with organizations connected to labour and industrial history, including the Brantford and District Labour Council, as well as international heritage networks such as the International Committee for the Conservation of Industrial Heritage (TICCIH). Partnerships have also extended to community and cultural associations in the Brantford area, including the Brantford Chinese Association and the Brantford Slavic Full Gospel Church, particularly through initiatives documenting the histories of immigrant communities in the region.
The centre’s activities have been supported by funding and assistance from several public and philanthropic organizations. Supporters have included the City of Brantford, the Ontario Trillium Foundation through its Resilient Communities Fund, the Brant Community Foundation, and programs of the Government of Canada, including the New Horizons for Seniors Program. Additional support has been provided by regional economic development organization Enterprise Brant.
These partnerships and sources of support have contributed to CIHC’s research initiatives, publications, community history projects, and digital heritage resources.
